title: "Why this repo is shaped like the exam blueprint"

date: 2026-08-31
categories: [Sprint]
---

The sprint starts on **2026-09-06**. This post is the pre-commitment: what the
plan is, and what it is deliberately getting wrong.

## The score report dictates the directory names

The CCAR-F result is not a single number. It reports pass/fail with a scaled
score **plus percent-correct by domain**. That detail is the whole design of this
repository: the five directories are numbered `01-` to `05-` to match the five
official domains exactly, so a weak domain N on the report points straight at
directory `0N-` with nothing to interpret in between.

| Directory | Domain | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| `01-agentic-loops/` | Agentic Architecture & Orchestration | **27%** |
| `02-mcp-servers/` | Tool Design & MCP Integration | 18% |
| `03-claude-code/` | Claude Code Configuration & Workflows | 20% |
| `04-prompt-engineering/` | Prompt Engineering & Structured Output | 20% |
| `05-context-reliability/` | Context Management & Reliability | 15% |

Domain 1 is 27% and carries 7 task statements — more of both than anything else.
Domain 5 carries the *lowest* weight at 15% and is nonetheless a primary domain
in **4 of the 6 exam scenarios**. It is connective tissue, not a corner case, and
the weighting understates it. Those two facts set the whole budget.

## Deadlines that GitHub will enforce

Twenty-six issues, each with a milestone carrying a real due date. Not a
checklist — a tracker that goes red.

The rule that makes it work is step 3 of the loop: **close the issue with a link
to the commit**. An issue closed with no artifact is a lie to your future self,
and a fortnight is more than long enough to start telling it.

## The sprint is over-committed, on purpose

56 hours are available. If every one of the 26 issues were a build, the work is
roughly 90 hours. That gap is not an oversight — it is the reason the issues sit
in three tiers:

- **10 core** issues — each owns its day and produces a committed artifact.
- **4 coverage-gap** issues — filed after auditing the blueprint and finding
  holes in Domains 1, 3 and 5. Each also owns a day.
- **12 secondary** issues — labelled `secondary`, each *sharing* a day with the
  topically closest primary issue. Reading and reasoning, not a separate build.

**If a day runs long, the secondary issue is what slips.** Naming the thing that
gives way in advance is the only way to stop the whole plan giving way instead.
Completion gets tracked against the 14 core-plus-gap issues; the 12 secondary
ones are a reading list with deadlines attached.

## Where it is already short

The allocation does not match the weighting, and the [sprint
plan](../../../sprint.qmd) shows the deltas rather than hiding them. The largest
shortfall is **Domain 4 at −3.2 h**, which is uncomfortable. All 30 statements
are tracked, but three of Domain 4's six (4.1, 4.2, 4.4) are tracked only by
`secondary` issues — the tier that shares a day and slips first. They are also
prompting fundamentals the sample questions lean on heavily. The least protected
work in the sprint is sitting on top of some of the most examinable material.

## What each of the next fourteen posts will contain

The same four headings, every day:

- **What I built** — with the issue number and the commit.
- **What surprised me** — the thing the docs did not say.
- **What I would get wrong on the exam** — stated before the mock, not after.
- **Time** — planned versus actual.

That last line is the one worth reading. A study plan's real finding is the
distance between what it budgeted and what it cost.
